summary: This informational memo lists functional requirements for supporting MPLS traffic engineering across routing areas. Solutions defining procedures and protocol extensions for it are expected to meet these requirements.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes what a solution for MPLS traffic engineering across routing areas should support. It also sets limits: a solution must preserve the separation and scalability that routing areas provide.

subtitle: Requirements for extending MPLS traffic engineering across multiple IGP areas.

tldr.problem: MPLS traffic engineering mechanisms described in the memo operate within one IGP area, while operators may need constrained paths and protection across areas.
tldr.mechanism: The memo states functional requirements for signaling, path computation, routing, recovery, interoperability, and evaluation, with mandatory and recommended levels.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4105 is a requirements document, not a protocol. It requires solutions to preserve IGP hierarchy and scalability while supporting inter-area traffic engineering.

today: RFC 4105 is Informational. The work-unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the memo states requirements for solutions rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: Why Traffic Engineering Across Areas
sections.content:
MPLS traffic engineering can establish explicitly routed label-switched paths that satisfy constraints. The memo describes uses within an area, including resource optimization, quality-of-service guarantees, and recovery from link, node, or shared-risk failures.

The document sets out requirements for extending these capabilities across multiple IGP areas. It distinguishes mandatory requirements from recommended ones because operators may have different needs. The memo applies to OSPF areas and IS-IS levels.
sections.plainLanguage: Within one routing area, an operator can choose paths to meet network goals. This memo says what a future solution should do when a path must cross area boundaries.

sections.title: The Existing Intra-Area Components
sections.content:
The memo describes three parts of intra-area MPLS traffic engineering. Link-state IGP extensions distribute traffic-engineering topology information. A constraint-based shortest-path computation at the head-end selects an LSP path. RSVP-TE signaling then establishes that LSP, including explicit routing, label distribution, and resource reservation.

Within an area, these mechanisms can move aggregate traffic away from overused resources, support QoS when combined with DiffServ mechanisms, and use backup LSPs for fast recovery. Traffic can be directed into LSPs through several routing approaches, including static routes and BGP recursive routing.
sections.plainLanguage: One part advertises network resources, one chooses a path, and one sets up the path. Together they can steer traffic and prepare for failures within an area.

sections.title: The Inter-Area Problem and Design Goals
sections.content:
Area hierarchy limits what a head-end router knows about topology outside its own area. Without information for the full route, it cannot run the same constrained path computation end to end. Running traffic engineering independently in each area can produce suboptimal resource use, cannot ensure an inter-area constrained shortest path, and does not provide local protection against an area-border-router failure.

A solution MUST preserve the IGP hierarchy and contain routing information. It MUST also preserve IGP and RSVP-TE scalability, avoiding unreasonable increases in information carried or flooding frequency. The requirements aim to extend traffic engineering without undoing the reasons the network was divided into areas.
sections.plainLanguage: A router cannot calculate a whole cross-area path if it sees only its own area. Any solution must exchange enough information to help, but not so much that area separation stops working.

sections.title: Signaling and Path Selection Requirements
sections.content:
A solution MUST establish inter-area TE LSPs using RSVP-TE and MUST interoperate with existing intra-area mechanisms. The head-end must be able to specify LSRs, including ABRs, as strict or loose hops. The solution SHOULD compute an optimal constrained path across areas, but the memo does not require every LSP to use an optimal route.

Path computation may expand a route area by area or compute an end-to-end path through cooperation between ABRs. If multiple methods are supported, operators should be able to select among them. Dynamic traffic-engineering topology information SHOULD remain within its area. Diversely routed LSPs MUST be supported for link, node, and SRLG diversity; crankback routing is optional and finds a feasible path rather than guaranteeing an optimum.
sections.plainLanguage: The head-end must be able to signal a path through areas, including chosen border routers. The path method should respect area boundaries and support different routes for protection when such routes exist.

sections.title: Recovery, Evaluation, and Security
sections.content:
A solution MUST support make-before-break reoptimization, rerouting after failures or preemption, and fast recovery for failures inside areas and at ABRs. It SHOULD support local and end-to-end reoptimization, hard and soft preemption, LSP nesting, mesh discovery, and fault-management mechanisms. Operators should be able to control specified behaviors on a per-LSP basis.

The memo evaluates solutions by path quality, setup time, scalability, complexity, and backward compatibility. It says the document introduces no new security issues beyond those inherent in MPLS TE, but administrative parameters must be changed securely by authorized entities.
sections.plainLanguage: A cross-area path should be repairable or moved to a better route without unnecessary disruption. Solutions are also judged by whether they remain manageable, scalable, and compatible with existing networks.
